sections.normalized_html:
First, we subtract the target number of gallons from the starting amount to find how much paint is used: [MATH: 6,900 - 1,236 = 5,664]

Next, we divide that amount by [MATH: 84] to find how many days it takes: [MATH: \frac{5,664}{84} = 67.42\ldots]

Since the number of days must be a whole number and the supply doesn’t reach the target until the full day is completed, we round up: [MATH: 68]

So, it will take [MATH: 68] days for the paint supply to reach [MATH: 1,236] gallons.

sections.normalized_html: During her marathon training, Mia runs [MATH: \dfrac{11}{20}] of the [MATH: 200] kilometers in her plan each week. If Mia keeps up this training pace, how many kilometers will she run in [MATH: 3] weeks?
sections.readable_text: During her marathon training, Mia runs [MATH: \dfrac{11}{20}] of the [MATH: 200] kilometers in her plan each week. If Mia keeps up this training pace, how many kilometers will she run in [MATH: 3] weeks?

sections.normalized_html:
First, we find how many kilometers Mia runs each week by taking [MATH: \dfrac{11}{20}] of [MATH: 200] kilometers. This gives

[MATH: \frac{11}{20} \times 200 = 110.]

So each week, Mia runs [MATH: 110] kilometers.

We can now find the total distance run in [MATH: 3] weeks to be

[MATH: 110 \times 3 = 330.]

Consequently, Mia will run [MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{330}] kilometers in [MATH: 3] weeks.
